records.sourceFile: Sports performance - is there evidence that the body clock plays a role.pdf

paper.citation: Reilly T, Waterhouse J. Sports performance: is there evidence that the body clock plays a role? Eur J Appl Physiol. 2009;106:321-332.
paper.abstract: Athletic performance shows a time-of-day effect with possible causes in environmental factors, the sleep-wake cycle and the internal body clock. The authors conclude that the body clock probably plays some role in sports performance rhythms, but the evidence does not separate it from time awake. They outline protocols to separate these roles and note that muscle fatigue is a serious barrier to experimental work.
paper.tldr: Sports performance follows a time-of-day pattern that peaks in the late afternoon, and the body clock probably contributes to it. Current evidence cannot yet say how much of the pattern is the body clock rather than time awake or the environment.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the time-of-day performance literature and chronobiological evidence, with suggested experimental protocols. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Many performance measures are higher in the late afternoon and early evening than in the morning. Reported rhythm peaks fall between about 15:30 and 20:30 hours, with amplitudes of 2 to 11 percent of the daily mean. The authors judge that the body clock probably plays some role, but the evidence is inconclusive.
paper.limitations: The authors describe much of the data as poor quality, and many studies compared only two times of day, so sampling was too infrequent to describe a circadian rhythm. Muscle fatigue makes rigorous protocols long or unacceptable, and the body clock and time awake cannot yet be separated.
paper.practicalImplications: When comparing athlete performance across the day, standardise and record test times, because the time of day alone can shift results. Where possible, test protocols should separate time awake from the body clock.
paper.athleteDev: Performance measures tend to peak in the late afternoon and early evening, so training and testing schedules could take time of day into account. This review cannot say how much of that rhythm is the body clock.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Sprint running- from fundamental mechanics to practice—a review.pdf

paper.citation: Haugen T, McGhie D, Ettema G. Sprint running: from fundamental mechanics to practice - a review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019.
paper.abstract: The authors examine sprint running literature using the mechanical principles that govern accelerated running. They discuss spring-mass models and their limits, the link between sprint mechanics and metabolic demand, and the emphasis on total and horizontal force. They argue that power analysis based on isolated end-goal force is flawed and discuss some practical concepts in sprint coaching.
paper.tldr: Sprint mechanics research can be misread when models or horizontal-force power figures are taken at face value. Coaches and analysts should check how a measure was derived before using it to explain sprint performance.
paper.methods: Invited narrative review of sprint running mechanics literature, interpreted through fundamental mechanical principles. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Spring-mass models describe gross sprint kinematics such as step length, step rate and contact time, but the authors argue they have flaws when applied to accelerated running. Analyses based on total and horizontal force, and power derived from isolated end-goal force, are argued to be limited or flawed. Metabolic models of sprinting are described as promising but still model based.
paper.limitations: The review is an argument rather than a systematic synthesis, and no search method is described. Its illustrative calculations use a few published data sets, and its views on practical sprint concepts are discussed rather than tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Check how a sprint model or force measure was derived before treating it as a mechanism. Interpret horizontal-force power figures obtained from isolated force data with caution.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest that sprint conditioning in most well-trained senior sprinters should target step rate, which they describe as the main within-athlete speed modulator, while longer step length, which requires strength, separates fast from intermediate sprinters. Model-based power figures should not be read as direct measures of an athlete's capacity.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation and cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria.

records.sourceFile: Sprint vs isolated eccentric training - Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Mendiguchia J, Conceição F, Edouard P, Fonseca M, Pereira R, Lopes H, et al. Sprint versus isolated eccentric training: Comparative effects on hamstring architecture and performance in soccer players. PLoS ONE. 2020;15(2):e0228283.
paper.abstract: The study compared Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint training, both added to regular soccer practice, on sprint performance, sprint mechanics and biceps femoris long head architecture. Six preseason weeks were compared across a soccer-only group, a Nordic group and a sprint group. The authors conclude that sprint training increased fascicle length more than Nordic training and also improved sprint performance and mechanics, while Nordic training did not improve sprint performance.
paper.tldr: Adding sprint training to a soccer preseason improved short sprint times and acceleration mechanics and increased hamstring fascicle length in this small sample. Injury protection was not measured, so the fascicle result should not be read as injury prevention.
paper.methods: Prospective randomised controlled study over six preseason weeks in 32 recruited soccer players who were allocated to three groups, with matching by position, playing status and previous hamstring injury. Nine players dropped out, leaving 23 analysed. Outcomes were 5 m and 20 m times and force-velocity mechanical outputs (F0, v0, Pmax, RFmax) from radar-measured 50 m sprints, and biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness by two-dimensional ultrasound, analysed with magnitude-based inference.
paper.findings: In the sprint group, sprint performance and mechanics showed small to large pre-post improvements, with only a small, possibly real gain in maximal velocity (v0). The sprint group showed a moderate increase in fascicle length (about 16 percent), compared with a smaller increase in the Nordic group (about 7 percent) and a trivial change in the soccer-only group. The soccer-only and Nordic groups showed trivial to small negative sprint changes, and only the Nordic group showed a small increase in pennation angle.
paper.limitations: Only 23 of 32 players were analysed, and the abstract reports the group sizes at recruitment (10, 12 and 10). Training and match load were not recorded, two-dimensional ultrasound has known limits for fascicle estimates, and injury outcomes were not measured. Between-group sprint comparisons with the soccer-only group were mostly trivial or unclear, and results rely on magnitude-based inference rather than hypothesis tests.
paper.practicalImplications: Sprint work within preseason soccer practice may improve short sprint times and acceleration mechanics over six weeks. Staff should not replace Nordic hamstring exercise with sprint work on the basis of this study, because injury protection was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: In this sample, sprint training within routine soccer practice improved 5 m and 20 m times and acceleration mechanics over six preseason weeks. Its effect on biceps femoris long head fascicle length was larger than that of the Nordic group.
paper.rtp: The study excluded players with recent hip, knee or lumbo-pelvic joint injury, used previous hamstring injury only as a matching variable, and did not measure return to play. It cannot show how sprint or Nordic training should guide return-to-sport decisions after a hamstring injury.

records.sourceFile: Strength training with intermittent blood flow restriction improved strength without changes in neural aspects on quadriceps muscle.pdf

paper.citation: de Castro FMP, Alves GF, Oliveira LP, Tourinho Filho H, Puggina EF. Strength training with intermittent blood flow restriction improved strength without changes in neural aspects on quadriceps muscle. Science & Sports. 2018 (article in press; volume and pages not printed).
paper.abstract: Low-intensity strength training with intermittent vascular occlusion increased muscle strength within the occlusion group in healthy resistance-trained men, while surface EMG measures of neural drive did not change over the training period.
paper.tldr: Six weeks of low-load knee extension training with cuff occlusion raised predicted 1RM within the occlusion group in trained men, but strength did not differ significantly from the non-occluded group and EMG neural measures did not change. Use it as weak evidence of a strength gain, not of a neural adaptation.
paper.methods: Twenty healthy resistance-trained men were randomized to low-load (20% predicted 1RM) unilateral knee extension with intermittent vascular occlusion (LIVO, n = 11) or without occlusion (LI, n = 9) for 6 weeks, 2 sessions per week, with the LI group matched to the LIVO group's repetition counts. Predicted 1RM and surface EMG (RMS and median frequency) of the vastus medialis and vastus lateralis were measured at weeks 1, 5 and 9, and EMG was also recorded in training sessions 1, 7 and 12.
paper.findings: The LIVO group's predicted 1RM increased in both legs (right 36.5 to 47.9 kg; left 35.9 to 47.4 kg), while the LI group's increase (right 29.9 to 37.9 kg; left 29.8 to 36.9 kg) was not significant; there were no between-group differences in predicted 1RM. RMS was higher in the LIVO group than the LI group in several sets during training sessions, but RMS and median frequency did not change between time points within either group.
paper.limitations: Small samples and a single unilateral exercise limit generalization. Predicted 1RM came from a repetitions-to-failure equation, not a measured maximum, and the LI group started with lower predicted 1RM. Hypertrophy was not measured, so the authors' suggestion that hypertrophy drove the gain is untested. The cuff pressure (mean 140 mmHg) may have altered motor unit recruitment and the EMG results.
paper.practicalImplications: For healthy resistance-trained men, low-load training with cuff occlusion was followed by a significant knee extension strength gain over 6 weeks, but it was not shown to outperform the same work without occlusion. The gain did not come with a measurable change in EMG neural measures, so this study does not support using occlusion to improve neural drive.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Low-load training with intermittent occlusion improved knee extension strength within the occlusion group in trained men over 6 weeks, and the authors argue, without measuring it, that hypertrophy is the more likely cause. Where strength without added muscle mass is the goal, the authors consider high-intensity training the more appropriate choice.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport loading. It tested healthy, resistance-trained men and included no injured or rehabilitating participants.

records.sourceFile: Strength, conditioning, and nutritional considerations for high-level performers.pdf

paper.citation: Kreider RB. Strength, conditioning, and nutritional considerations for high-level performers. Kinesiology Review. 2020;9(1):31-40.
paper.abstract: Describes the history, professional preparation, program components and general principles of strength and conditioning and sport nutrition, their impact on high-level performance, and future trends in these fields.
paper.tldr: A practitioner overview of how strength and conditioning and sport nutrition support high-level athletes, with general energy and macronutrient ranges by sport type. It is a narrative summary, not a systematic review of the evidence.
paper.methods: Narrative overview by one author. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or evidence-grading method for the reviewed literature is described.
paper.findings: The paper describes training principles (specificity, overload, progression and variation) and periodization phases, and cites studies in which multi-component programs improved strength, power and speed in male and female athletes. It gives recommended energy intakes (for example 45 to 60 kcal/kg/day for strength and power athletes) and carbohydrate and protein ranges by sport type (Table 2). It reports the ISSN classification in which creatine monohydrate, essential amino acids and protein (plus calcium HMB in untrained people) have strong evidence for muscle-mass gains during training, and beta-alanine, caffeine, carbohydrate, creatine, sodium bicarbonate, sodium phosphate, water and glucose electrolyte drinks, and energy drinks have strong evidence for performance (Tables 3 and 4).
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so it cannot be used to judge how complete the evidence is. Several figures, such as energy ranges, are general guidance and are not derived from the studies in the paper. The author discloses grants, consulting and expert witness roles.
paper.practicalImplications: Strength and power athletes often need high energy intakes (45 to 60 kcal/kg/day) with carbohydrate and protein set by sport and training load, according to the author's ranges. Supplements should be chosen by evidence grade, legality in the sport, and third-party banned-substance testing.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Periodized training that varies exercise type and volume, combined with the energy and macronutrient ranges in Table 2, provides a framework for planning high-level athlete programs. The ISSN evidence tiers can help screen supplements before use.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport. It contains no rehabilitation or injury-specific evidence, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play loading or nutrition.

records.sourceFile: Tackle Height and Tackle Success—An Analysis of 52,204 Tackle Events.pdf

paper.citation: Hendricks S, Till K, Scantlebury S, et al. Tackle Height and Tackle Success - An Analysis of 52,204 Tackle Events. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025; 25:e70003.
paper.abstract: The authors compared the probability of tackle success when the tackler first contacted the ball-carrier at the shoulder, mid-torso or legs, for active, passive, smother and arm tackles, across seven male playing groups. Video of 271 matches was analysed with multilevel logistic regression that adjusted for tackle direction, sequence, number of tacklers and attacking intention. Active shoulder tackles had the highest success probability across levels, and arm tackles the lowest.
paper.tldr: Active shoulder and smother tackles were the most successful tackle types at every level from U16 upward, and arm tackles were the least successful. Shoulder contact beat mid-torso contact in the junior groups, but the senior difference was only a few percentage points.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional video analysis of competitive male rugby matches coded with a consensus video framework. Tackle success was modelled with multilevel logistic regression (random effects for country and match), with tackle type and first contact point as the main terms and situational covariates held at observed values. Separate models were fitted for each playing group, and adjusted probabilities were reported with 95% CIs.
paper.findings: At Senior Elite, the adjusted success probability for active shoulder tackles was 86% at the shoulder, 82% at mid-torso and 78% at the legs; arm tackles were 75%, 69% and 65%. From U16 upward, active shoulder and smother tackles had the highest and similar success probabilities, although Table 4 shows a small significant gap at U18 Amateur (3 to 4 points, p = 0.043). In Table 3, shoulder contact beat mid-torso contact at every level (4 to 9 points), and at U12, U14 and U16 leg contact also beat mid-torso contact.
paper.limitations: The abstract and text describe no difference between shoulder and mid-torso contact at senior levels, but Table 3 reports significant differences of about 4 percentage points at Senior Elite and Senior Amateur (p less than 0.001 for most tackle types); this report follows the table values. The text also says active shoulder and smother tackles did not differ from U16 upward (p greater than 0.05), while Table 4 gives p = 0.043 at U18 Amateur. The title gives 52,204 tackles, the abstract and methods give 51,106, and the stated 271 matches does not match the group counts, which sum to 266. Only male players were studied, ball-carrier body position was not coded, and tackle success was dichotomised.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can use the tackle-type ranking in training, with smother tackles treated as equal in importance to active shoulder tackles from U16. Contact-height advice should weigh the small senior performance gap against the safety rationale the authors give for mid-torso contact.
paper.athleteDev: Success rates differ by age group, so tackle training can target the contact point and tackle type that are most successful for each age group. The authors suggest greater emphasis on teaching the smother tackle, which has fewer standardised technical criteria than the active shoulder tackle.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study measures tackle success in match video and does not assess injury, recovery or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Taking the plunge - When is best for hot water immersion to complement exercise in heat and hypoxia.pdf

paper.citation: Dennis MC, Goods PSR, Binnie MJ, Girard O, Wallman KE, Dawson BT, et al. Taking the plunge: When is best for hot water immersion to complement exercise in heat and hypoxia. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
paper.abstract: Ten recreationally active men completed three repeated-sprint sessions in hypoxia at 40 C and about 3000 m simulated altitude, with hot water immersion (HWI) before the session (PRE), after it (POST), or with no immersion (CON). PRE lowered power output in every sprint set and raised core temperature, while POST matched CON for power output and core temperature during exercise and gave a higher core temperature at the end of the post-exercise period.
paper.tldr: Hot water immersion after a repeated-sprint session in the heat kept power output at control levels while adding heat load. Immersion before the session cut sprint power by about 15 to 17 percent.
paper.methods: Ten recreationally active men completed a familiarisation and three randomised trials, each with 3 x 10 x 5-s all-out sprints in a heat and hypoxia chamber (40 C, 50% RH, FIO2 0.144). Each trial had 30 min of either hot water immersion at 40 C or seated rest at 21 C before and after exercise. Core temperature, power output, heart rate, thermal sensation and RPE were recorded and analysed with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: PRE reduced mean power, peak power and total work by 14.8 to 16.8 percent versus POST and CON (all p < 0.001), with PRE core temperature higher during the pre-exercise period and exercise (p < 0.001 and p = 0.025). Time at 38.5 C or above was 48.1 +/- 22.5 min in PRE, 31.0 +/- 11.3 min in POST and 15.8 +/- 16.3 min in CON. POST power output and core temperature during exercise were similar to CON, and thermal sensation during exercise did not differ between conditions.
paper.limitations: The effects were acute, so chronic heat acclimation and training effects could not be assessed. Core temperature could not be measured after the post-exercise immersion ended, so the full heat dose of POST is an estimate. Participants were recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and fitness was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In a heat and hypoxia repeated-sprint session, placing hot water immersion after the session preserved sprint output while adding heat strain. Placing it before the session reduced sprint output, so it should not be used before high-intensity sprint work.
paper.athleteDev: Post-session hot water immersion (30 min at 40 C) can add heat stress to a repeated-sprint session in hypoxia without reducing sprint power output in this sample. Its effect over repeated weeks is not known.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy, recreationally active men in one acute session and included no injured athletes or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The Association Between Training Load and Performance in Team Sports- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Fox JL, Stanton R, Sargent C, Wintour SA, Scanlan AT. The Association Between Training Load and Performance in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically searched PubMed, SPORTDiscus and PsycINFO for original research in team sports on training load and performance. Of 26 included studies, the authors found that heart rate-based high-intensity training load and the individualized training impulse model were associated with aerobic performance, while other load measures showed weak or no clear associations with aerobic, neuromuscular or game-related outcomes.
paper.tldr: In team sports, the heart rate-based high-intensity training load is the training measure most consistently linked to aerobic gains. Other external load measures and session RPE show weak or no consistent links to performance.
paper.methods: Systematic review of original research in PubMed, SPORTDiscus and PsycINFO to July 2018. Two authors assessed quality with the Downs and Black checklist, and the lead author extracted the data. The review did not pool effect sizes or run a meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Twenty-six studies met the inclusion criteria, with quality scores from 6 to 10 out of 11. Training exposure was more strongly associated with aerobic performance than other external load measures, and high-intensity activity (90% of maximum heart rate or above) and the individualized training impulse model were strongly associated with aerobic performance. Other training impulse models and perceptual load measures showed weak associations, and there were no clear associations with neuromuscular variables or game-related statistics.
paper.limitations: Many studies were small, most used soccer players, and the statistical analyses varied widely, so direct comparison between studies was difficult and effect sizes could not be pooled. Several studies reported only effect sizes or only significance, and all studies linking high-intensity activity to aerobic performance were in field-based sports, so the authors say application to court-based sports needs more work.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches should use heart rate-based high-intensity training load when aiming to improve aerobic capacity, and should be cautious about using session RPE, external load or common training impulse models to predict performance changes in team sports.
paper.athleteDev: For team sport athletes, the review supports monitoring time spent at or above 90% of maximum heart rate to track aerobic development. It gives weak support for using session RPE or external load alone to predict changes in performance.
paper.rtp: This review does not study injured athletes or return to sport and cannot be used to set return-to-play training loads.

records.sourceFile: The Braking Performance Framework - Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports.pdf

paper.citation: Harper DJ, Cervantes C, Van Dyke M, Evans M, McBurnie AJ, Dos Santos T, et al. The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
paper.abstract: The article proposes a Braking Performance Framework to guide the choice of training methods for horizontal deceleration. It sets out exercises built on the known neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of braking, with practical programming guidelines for practitioners.
paper.tldr: Horizontal deceleration can be trained with eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction exercises, sequenced by the athlete's needs. The authors offer practical programming guidelines drawn from existing evidence, which is limited for several methods.
paper.methods: Narrative review and practical framework, with no described literature search. The authors draw on the known determinants of horizontal deceleration and on published studies of eccentric, isometric, flywheel, plyometric and change-of-direction training to propose exercise categories and programming tables.
paper.findings: The authors propose a framework with three exercise categories: braking elementary exercises that build eccentric and tissue capacity, braking development exercises that target fast eccentric and concentric force and rate of force development, and braking performance exercises that train deceleration under game-like perceptual demands. They give programming guidance, such as in-season flywheel scheduling, and note limited research on heavy assisted braking steps and an unknown minimum effective dose for supplementary deceleration training.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors acknowledge that the dose-response relationships and the effects of several exercise types are not well established, so many recommendations are expert judgement.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners can use the framework to choose and progress braking exercises, moving from elementary eccentric and isometric work through development exercises toward unanticipated and game-specific decelerations. Progressions should be checked against the athlete's response, since dose-response evidence is limited.
paper.athleteDev: Use the framework to target the eccentric and isometric determinants of deceleration, then progress toward braking in change-of-direction and game-like tasks. Adjust volume and intensity using the athlete's response, because the dose-response evidence is limited.
paper.rtp: The framework is written for healthy athletes preparing for multi-directional sport, and the authors do not present it as a return-to-sport protocol. Use it for return-to-sport planning only with clinical judgement, because it has not been tested in injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The Correlations Between Training Load Parameters and Physical Performance Adaptations in Team Sports - A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Clemente FM, Scanlan AT, Ramirez-Campillo R, Martinho D, Thapa RK, Chamari K, et al. The Correlations Between Training Load Parameters and Physical Performance Adaptations in Team Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:156.
paper.abstract: The authors searched four databases for team sport studies with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post performance tests. Of 40 studies with 726 players, heart rate-based training impulse correlated with endurance adaptations (r = 0.43 to 0.63), and session RPE and external load showed limited associations with performance adaptations.
paper.tldr: In team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the training load measure most closely linked to endurance gains. Session RPE and external load show weak links to performance adaptations, and the evidence is of very low certainty.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science, with an updated search in September 2025. Eligible studies included men or women in team sports at trained or developmental level with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post physical testing. Pooled correlations used random effects, study quality used the Downs and Black scale, and certainty used GRADE.
paper.findings: Forty studies with 726 players were included, 27 of them in soccer and 4 in women only. Heart rate-based training impulse correlated with changes in maximal oxygen uptake (r = 0.63), velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.47) and velocity at onset of blood lactate accumulation (r = 0.43), while session RPE correlated with changes in velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.29) and showed a small correlation with sprint changes over more than 10 m (r = -0.23). Strength and jump power changes were not associated with training load, and all analyses were rated very low certainty under GRADE.
paper.limitations: The authors note uneven coverage of the literature, with most external load studies in outdoor sports such as soccer and rugby, few indoor sport studies, and only four studies in women. All analyses were downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, falling well below the optimal sample size of 800 participants, and some also for heterogeneity.
paper.practicalImplications: Use heart rate-based training impulse when tracking endurance adaptations in team sport players. Do not rely on session RPE or external load alone to predict strength, power or speed gains, and treat the pooled correlations as a guide rather than a prescription.
paper.athleteDev: For team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the most consistent training load signal for endurance development, such as VO2max and lactate thresholds. Strength, power and speed should be tracked with direct testing, since external and session load show weak links to them.
paper.rtp: The review covers healthy team sport players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

records.sourceFile: The Dose–Response of the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Biceps Femoris Architecture and Eccentric Knee Flexor Strength_- A Randomized Interventional Trial.pdf

paper.citation: Behan FP, Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, Timmins RG, Ruddy JD, Opar DA. The Dose-Response of the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Biceps Femoris Architecture and Eccentric Knee Flexor Strength: A Randomized Interventional Trial. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: In 40 recreationally active men, six weeks of Nordic hamstring exercise at four volume patterns was compared for biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric knee flexor strength. Initial high volume followed by low volume, and progressively increasing volume, raised both outcomes; low volume raised strength but not fascicle length.
paper.tldr: In recreationally active men, a high-volume start followed by low volume, or steadily rising volume, increased hamstring fascicle length and eccentric strength over 6 weeks. Weekly low volume (48 total reps) increased strength but not fascicle length, and 8 reps every second week (24 total) changed neither.
paper.methods: Forty recreationally active males were randomised to four 6-week NHE protocols with supervised sessions on 0 to 3 days per week, followed by 4 weeks of detraining. Weekly B-mode ultrasound measured biceps femoris long head fascicle length and pennation angle, and eccentric knee flexor strength was measured on a Nordbord device at baseline, posttest and during detraining; linear mixed models were used.
paper.findings: After 6 weeks, fascicle length increased in group 3 (+0.83 cm, +7%, P = .027) and group 4 (+1.48 cm, +14%, P = .004), and pennation angle fell in groups 3 and 4. Eccentric strength increased in groups 2 (+53.6 N, +14%), 3 (+63.4 N, +17%) and 4 (+74.7 N, +19%), with no significant change reported for group 1. Group 4 was stronger than group 1 at posttest (+94.2 N). After 4 weeks of detraining, fascicle length had returned to baseline in groups 3 and 4, and group 3 strength fell significantly (-33.9 N) while group 4 kept its gains.
paper.limitations: Groups of 10 recreationally active men; no untrained control group; fascicle length is an estimate. The abstract says strength returned to baseline in group 2 after detraining, but the results report no post hoc test for group 2 at that stage.
paper.practicalImplications: Include at least one NHE session each week to keep eccentric strength rising. In this study, fascicle-length gains came only from the higher-volume protocols (176 or 358 total reps over 6 weeks), while 24 or 48 total reps did not change fascicle length.
paper.athleteDev: Keep the NHE at least once weekly to maintain eccentric strength, and use an early higher-volume block if fascicle length is the goal. A 4-week break can erase fascicle-length gains, so plan maintenance exposure through the season.
paper.rtp: Healthy recreationally active men only; no injured participants and no return-to-sport or re-injury outcome. It cannot set return-to-play loads or show that any protocol lowers hamstring injury risk, although the strength and architecture changes are relevant to later preventive planning.

records.sourceFile: The Efect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations- A Systematic Review and Meta‑analyses.pdf

paper.citation: Cuthbert M, Ripley N, McMahon JJ, Evans M, Haff GG, Comfort P. The Effect of Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention Volume on Eccentric Strength and Muscle Architecture Adaptations: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on how Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) training volume relates to eccentric hamstring strength and biceps femoris architecture. Pre-post effects were large across high and low volumes after 6 or more weeks, and volume alone did not show a clear trend.
paper.tldr: Across studies, NHE protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large strength and fascicle gains at both high and low volumes. Lower, consistent volumes may suit squads where soreness limits compliance.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided search of three databases (293 records) to 1 December 2018; 13 studies with at least 4 weeks of NHE, pre-post means and SDs, and biceps femoris architecture data were included. Study quality was rated with TESTEX, risk of bias with the Cochrane tool for the RCTs and publication bias with a Rosenthal fail-safe N; Hedges' g values were calculated within studies and a random-effects model estimated between-study effects.
paper.findings: After 6 or more weeks, both high and low volume protocols produced large to very large within-study gains in eccentric strength, and three fascicle length measures showed very large gains (g of 2.58 or more). Weekly volumes ranged from about 21 to 73 repetitions with no clear volume trend. Studies of 4 weeks showed trivial to small change, and control groups showed trivial or negative change (g of 0.14 or less).
paper.limitations: Only 13 studies, two without a control group; several studies had low TESTEX scores and did not report compliance or blinded assessment; the review was not pre-registered; the volume conclusion rests on uncontrolled pre-post effects. The abstract gives g = 2.12 (high volume) and g = 2.28 (low volume) for strength, but the results attribute g = 2.12 to a single study of eccentric peak torque and do not report g = 2.28.
paper.practicalImplications: Protocols of 6 or more weeks produced large gains in the included studies, and volume did not clearly change the result. Where soreness drives poor adherence, a lower and consistent weekly volume may be a reasonable option, with intensity progressed over time.
paper.athleteDev: Run NHE blocks for at least 6 weeks, progress the exercise's intensity rather than adding volume, and track compliance. A lower consistent volume may suit squads where soreness limits adherence.
paper.rtp: The review contains no injured athletes and does not measure return to sport or injury outcomes. Strength and fascicle changes are surrogate outcomes for injury risk, so it cannot show that any NHE volume reduces re-injury or sets return-to-sport loads.

records.sourceFile: The Efectiveness of Resisted Sled Training (RST) for Sprint Performance- A Systematic Review and Meta‑analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Alcaraz PE, Carlos-Vivas J, Oponjuru BO, Martinez-Rodriguez A. The Effectiveness of Resisted Sled Training (RST) for Sprint Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on resisted sled training and sprint time. Sled training improved early acceleration and full-sprint times pre-post, did not improve maximum-velocity sprint time, and was not better than sprinting without a sled.
paper.tldr: Sled sprint training improved early acceleration in recreationally active and trained athletes, but it was no better than the same sprinting without a sled, and maximum-velocity sprint time did not improve significantly. The authors recommend 6 or more weeks at 2 to 3 sessions a week.
paper.methods: Systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to January 2018 with PRISMA reporting; 13 studies (32 RST groups, 15 control groups) with sprint time data at 10 m (acceleration), 15 m or more (maximum velocity) and 20 m or more (full sprint). Quality was rated with PEDro (mean 8 of 10), and random-effects pooled effect sizes with subgroup analyses were calculated.
paper.findings: Pre-post sprint time improved in the acceleration phase (ES 0.61, P = .0001; heterogeneity I2 = 28%) and full sprint (ES 0.36, P = .009), but not in the maximum-velocity phase (ES 0.27, P = .25). Studies with control groups showed no significant RST-versus-control difference in any phase (acceleration ES 0.09, P = .64). Acceleration effects were moderate in recreationally active (ES 0.75) and trained (ES 0.84) participants but small and non-significant in highly trained ones (ES 0.30) and in female samples (ES 0.14); loads below and above 20% of body mass gave similar effects (0.61 vs 0.63), though the higher-load effect was not significant.
paper.limitations: Subgroup comparisons rest on few studies and are not controlled comparisons; the frequency result comes from one study; the pooled sample for maximum velocity is small (81 participants); the bias check was visual.
paper.practicalImplications: For early acceleration in team sports, use a block of at least 6 weeks at 2 to 3 sessions a week, with about 160 m or more per session in the studies that showed the largest effects. Do not expect a top-speed gain from sled work, and keep sled loads near or below about 20% of body mass for sprint-replication work.
paper.athleteDev: For early acceleration in soccer or rugby, a 6-week sled block at 2 to 3 sessions a week improved sprint times in the pooled studies, though unresisted sprinting did about as well. For top speed the review found no significant effect, and the authors suggest that vertical-force methods such as plyometrics may be needed.
paper.rtp: Only healthy, at least recreationally active participants; no injured athletes and no injury or return-to-sport outcome. Sprint-time gains cannot be used to judge readiness to sprint after injury or to set graded return loads.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of A Flywheel Hip Extension Vs A Traditional Hip Extension Exercise on Hamstring Strength.pdf

paper.citation: O Brien J, Browne D, Earls D, Lodge C. The Effect of A Flywheel Hip Extension Vs A Traditional Hip Extension Exercise on Hamstring Strength. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.
paper.abstract: Twenty U-20 male soccer players did six weeks of either flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift twice weekly. Both improved 3RM deadlift strength; only the flywheel group showed a significant gain in eccentric hamstring strength, and the authors describe its gain as superior.
paper.tldr: In U-20 soccer players, six weeks of flywheel or traditional Romanian deadlift both raised 3RM strength. Only the flywheel version showed a significant eccentric hamstring gain, but the groups did not differ significantly on that outcome, so a flywheel advantage is not established.
paper.methods: Random allocation to flywheel RDL (inertial load set by a power test; 4 sets of 6 with two extra submaximal pre-repetitions) or traditional RDL (80% of predicted 1RM), twice weekly for 6 weeks with matched set-RPE 8. Outcomes were 3RM RDL and peak eccentric force during the NHE on a Hamstring Solo device before and after training, analysed with a 2 x 2 group x time repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Eccentric strength rose 13% (37 N, P = .03, g = 0.51) in the flywheel group but 5% (14 N, P = .282) in the traditional group; the time x group interaction for eccentric strength was not significant (P = .18). 3RM rose 18% (19 kg, g = 1.07) in the flywheel group and 28% (26 kg, g = 0.99) in the traditional group, with a significant time x group interaction (P = .02) favouring the traditional group's larger gain.
paper.limitations: No control group, six weeks only, small groups, and usual training was not controlled. The abstract and discussion describe superior eccentric gains for flywheel, but the interaction test was not significant (P = .18). The text effect sizes (g = 0.18, 0.51, 0.99 and 1.07) also differ slightly from Table 2 (0.2, 0.53, 1.0 and 1.11).
paper.practicalImplications: Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build 3RM Romanian deadlift strength in youth soccer players over 6 weeks. The flywheel version may add an eccentric hamstring gain, but this trial does not show that it is better than a traditional RDL for that outcome.
paper.athleteDev: Either flywheel or traditional RDL can build hip extension strength in youth players. Use the flywheel version if an eccentric gain is the goal, with the caveat that the group difference was not significant, and match intensity with set-RPE.
paper.rtp: Players were healthy and uninjured; no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcome were studied. It is a strength-block study, so it cannot set return-to-sport loads or show reduced re-injury.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of a Synthetic-Grass Sport Surface on Physiology and Perception During Intermittent Exercise in Hot Conditions.pdf

paper.citation: Singh G, Bennett KJM, McGuigan H, Goddard SG, Stevens CJ. The Effect of a Synthetic-Grass Sport Surface on Physiology and Perception During Intermittent Exercise in Hot Conditions. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2024. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Randomized crossover study of 13 team-sport athletes running intermittently for 50 minutes on synthetic and natural grass in hot conditions. Skin temperature, sweat rate and thermal sensation were higher on synthetic grass, while the change in core temperature, heart rate and effort did not differ.
paper.tldr: Synthetic turf in hot conditions raised skin temperature, sweat rate and perceived heat in this group of athletes, but the rise in core temperature, heart rate and effort matched natural grass. Expect athletes to feel hotter on turf without assuming a larger core-temperature rise.
paper.methods: Thirteen athletes (9 male, 4 female) completed two 50-minute standardized intermittent running protocols on synthetic and natural grass, a week apart, in a counterbalanced crossover design. Core temperature was measured with an ingestible telemetric capsule, and skin temperature, heart rate, sweat rate, RPE, thermal sensation and thermal comfort were recorded.
paper.findings: Final skin temperature was higher on synthetic grass at the calf (40.1 vs 33.4 C), shoulder (36.6 vs 33.7 C) and chest (33.2 vs 31.8 C), and sweat rate was higher (1.5 vs 1.2 L per hour). Final core temperature was slightly higher on natural grass (38.4 vs 38.2 C, P=0.042), but the change in core temperature (1.3 vs 1.4 C) and heart rate, thermal comfort and RPE did not differ between surfaces.
paper.limitations: Only 13 athletes were tested, and the authors note they were likely partly acclimatized from the Australian summer. Air and surface temperatures were measured higher over synthetic grass (Table 1), so the two surfaces were not identical environments. Results may not transfer to unacclimatized athletes, other sports or longer sessions, and performance was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: The study supports treating synthetic grass in heat as a thermal-comfort and skin-temperature issue, since athletes felt hotter and sweated more on it. It does not show a larger core-temperature rise, heart rate increase or effort increase, so this study alone does not justify changing session plans on turf.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the surface alone did not change core temperature, heart rate or effort in a 50-minute session, so it is not a reason on its own to cut training intensity. Sweat rate and thermal sensation were higher on synthetic grass, and the effect on performance remains unknown.
paper.rtp: The study used one session per surface in trained or developmental athletes and did not measure injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer - A Session-to-Session Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Tan B, Hu A, Zheng Y. The Impact of Weekly Acceleration and Deceleration Loads on Neuromuscular Performance in Soccer: A Session-to-Session Analysis. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2025;24:851-860.
paper.abstract: This study examined weekly variations in accelerations, decelerations and neuromuscular performance in male under-19 soccer players, and whether accumulated acceleration and deceleration loads relate to neuromuscular changes across a weekly microcycle. Thirty-nine outfield players were monitored by GNSS over two consecutive weeks, with countermovement jump (CMJ), hamstring strength (HS) and delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) measured before and after training. CMJ and HS fell significantly after training on all five days, most on MD-4 and MD-5, and DOMS peaked on MD-3. No significant correlations were found between daily acceleration or deceleration counts and changes in CMJ or HS.
paper.tldr: In 39 under-19 players, CMJ and hamstring strength fell after training on every day and were lowest on MD-4 and MD-5, but single-day acceleration and deceleration counts did not predict those drops. Plan late-week loads using the cumulative pattern rather than one session's counts.
paper.methods: Descriptive, repeated-measures observational study over two consecutive weeks with two under-19 teams in provincial competition. Accelerations and decelerations were counted by a 10 Hz GNSS vest for each training session. CMJ height and isometric hamstring strength were measured 30 minutes before and 15 minutes after each session, and a 0 to 6 DOMS scale was completed each morning before training. Values were averaged by day relative to match day, then analysed with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc tests and Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: Post-training CMJ and hamstring strength were significantly below pre-training on every day (p < 0.001). The largest drops were on MD-4 (CMJ -7.9%, hamstring -7.9%) and MD-5 (CMJ -7.8%, hamstring -7.9%). Pre-training CMJ and hamstring strength declined from MD-1 to MD-4. DOMS peaked on MD-3 (mean 1.04). Acceleration and deceleration counts were highest on MD-4 (means 44.00 and 43.65). No daily count was significantly correlated with the post-pre change in CMJ or HS; MD-5 showed non-significant trends of r = -0.27 to -0.32 (p = 0.050 to 0.092).
paper.limitations: Observational design with no control group, so the findings describe association only. The sample is modest, restricted to two youth male teams, and chosen by convenience; daily values were averaged across the two weeks, only two trials per test were used, and only acceleration and deceleration counts were analysed. The text has internal inconsistencies: it says MD-5 sessions produced relatively few accelerations and that pre-training MD-5 CMJ and HS were lower than MD-1 to MD-4, but Tables 1 and 3 show MD-5 pre-training values close to MD-1 and the second-highest acceleration counts; table values are reported here. Planned next-day DOMS correlations are not reported, and the MD-5 correlation trends did not reach significance.
paper.practicalImplications: Track CMJ and hamstring strength before and after sessions across the week, and plan MD-4 and MD-5 loads with recovery in mind, since those were the lowest-performing days in this group. Do not use a single session's acceleration or deceleration count to predict same-day decline, because this study found no link. Combine GNSS counts with other load and wellness measures.
paper.athleteDev: Use pre- and post-session CMJ and hamstring tests as a weekly fatigue check, and watch midweek soreness, which peaked on MD-3 here. Do not use session acceleration or deceleration counts alone to judge an individual player's same-day readiness, since the study found no relationship.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. Players recovering from injury were excluded, so the results cannot set return-to-play criteria or load limits for injured players.
